operationalization: Measure the frequency of morphologically intermediate forms within stratigraphically resolved clades across stages of single geological formations, and check taxonomic assignments in paleontological databases to see whether stage-separated intermediates are ranked as distinct species rather than varieties.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Stratigraphic occurrences and taxonomic ranks of fossil taxa across stages within geological formations

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Discrete character matrices for fossil clades to quantify morphological intermediacy between stratigraphic stages

obstacles: What counts as a 'transitional link' or 'only a few' is qualitative and depends on character sampling.
Taxonomic rank assignment in paleontology conflates genuine evolutionary divergence with taxonomic convention across stratigraphic boundaries.
rationale: Whether paleontologists rank closely related forms from different stages as distinct species can be evaluated directly from taxonomic and stratigraphic databases, and morphometric series exist for microfossils and invertebrates. However, Darwin's prediction that 'only a few' links should be found is loosely bounded and difficult to separate from competing models of punctuated stasis versus gradualism.

operationalization: Compare historical first-appearance datums (FADs) of genera, families, and orders across successive editions of global fossil compilations or discovery-year records to test whether continued sampling systematically pushes first appearances into older strata, and compare stratigraphic FADs with phylogenetic ghost lineage durations.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Stratigraphic ages and publication years of fossil occurrences to track downward range extensions over time

candidate_datasets.name: Macrostrat
candidate_datasets.role: Stratigraphic hiatuses and rock volume availability underlying apparent sudden appearances

obstacles: Some rapid diversifications reflect genuine evolutionary radiations rather than purely preservational artefacts.
Taxonomic revisions over time alter the definition of higher groups independently of new fossil discoveries.
rationale: This prediction is readily operationalized by tracking downward stratigraphic range extensions as discovery effort increases and by testing whether simultaneous first appearances correlate with sequence-stratigraphic unconformities. Public paleontological databases contain timestamped occurrence records and rock-record metrics that allow a direct quantitative test.

operationalization: Estimate stem-lineage duration prior to the acquisition of major ecological innovations (such as powered flight in birds, bats, pterosaurs, and insects) relative to the subsequent crown-group diversification rate and geographic range expansion using dated phylogenies and fossil occurrences.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: First appearances, species richness trajectories, and paleogeographic spread of clades with novel life modes

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Character matrices for tip-dating and estimating evolutionary rates along stem versus crown branches

obstacles: Stem lineages of flying groups such as bats and pterosaurs have notoriously poor fossil preservation, making the duration of initial adaptation uncertain.
Separating intrinsic key-innovation effects from extrinsic ecological opportunity after mass extinctions is difficult.
rationale: Macroevolutionary rate shifts following key innovations can be tested with dated phylogenies and fossil occurrence data. However, because early transitional stages in groups like bats and pterosaurs are sparsely preserved, comparing the time needed to evolve the novelty against the subsequent radiation relies heavily on molecular clock and ghost-lineage assumptions.

operationalization: Compare the radiometric duration of the fossiliferous Precambrian (Archean and Proterozoic eons) with the Phanerozoic (Cambrian/Silurian to present), and evaluate the global stratigraphic and geochemical record of Precambrian life.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Global occurrences of Ediacaran, Proterozoic, and Archean fossils and stromatolites

candidate_datasets.name: Macrostrat
candidate_datasets.role: Geochronological durations and distributions of Precambrian versus Phanerozoic sedimentary units

obstacles: Interpreting whether predominantly microbial and Ediacaran ecosystems satisfy Darwin's phrase 'swarmed with living creatures' involves minor semantic latitude.
rationale: Darwin's prediction divides cleanly into a geochronological question (whether pre-Cambrian time with life exceeded post-Cambrian time) and a paleobiological question (whether life was abundant during that interval). Radiometric dating and Precambrian microfossil, stromatolite, and Ediacaran records in public databases resolve both parts decisively.

operationalization: Compare paleomagnetic, marine geophysical, and paleogeographic reconstructions of continental and oceanic crust since the Early Paleozoic against present-day continent and ocean basin positions, and check the maximum age of oceanic crust and islands.

candidate_datasets.name: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information
candidate_datasets.role: Global marine geophysical and ocean-crustal age grids showing no oceanic crust older than the Mesozoic

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Paleocoordinates of Paleozoic and Mesozoic fossil localities relative to modern continental positions

obstacles: Darwin's phrase 'occupied their present areas' is somewhat ambiguous between cratonic permanence (crustal identity) and fixed geographic coordinates.
rationale: Darwin's historical inference that continents and oceans have remained roughly in their present positions since the Silurian can be directly tested and refuted by modern plate tectonic, paleomagnetic, and ocean-floor age datasets. Public geophysical and paleogeographic datasets clearly resolve both the young age of oceanic islands and the large-scale drift and reorganization of continents.

operationalization: Test whether first appearances of terrestrial and marine fossil species are distributed across stratigraphic intervals rather than concentrated exclusively at discrete stage boundaries, after controlling for sequence-stratigraphic hiatuses and sampling intensity.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: First appearance datums of marine and terrestrial species across geological time bins

candidate_datasets.name: Neotoma Paleoecology Database
candidate_datasets.role: High-resolution late Cenozoic terrestrial and aquatic fossil records

obstacles: Unconformities and stage-level binning in global databases artificially cluster first appearances at interval boundaries.
Coordinated turnover pulses (turnover-pulse hypothesis) can produce partially clustered origination.
rationale: Testing continuous versus batch-wise origination of species is a standard macroevolutionary analysis using fossil occurrence databases. High-resolution Cenozoic marine and terrestrial sections provide sufficient temporal resolution to evaluate whether species appear successively rather than in simultaneous global batches.

operationalization: Compare species durations (longevities), taxonomic turnover rates, and morphological evolutionary rates across genera and classes in the fossil record using survival analysis and phylogenetic comparative methods.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Stratigraphic ranges of fossil species and genera across classes to estimate turnover and longevity distributions

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Morphological character matrices across clades to compare rates of character change

obstacles: Taxonomic practices differ across classes (e.g., mammal teeth versus bivalve shells), which can inflate apparent rate differences.
rationale: Differences in evolutionary rates and species durations across genera and classes are classic paleobiological metrics (such as Simpson's horotely, bradytely, and tachytely). Public fossil databases have extensive taxonomic and temporal coverage to confirm large, statistically robust differences in turnover and morphological change among clades.

operationalization: Compare median species and genus stratigraphic durations and per-million-year origination and extinction rates between terrestrial and marine clades in the fossil record.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Environmental assignments (marine vs. terrestrial) and stratigraphic ranges of fossil species and genera

obstacles: Terrestrial fossil preservation is much more episodic and spatially restricted than marine preservation, which truncates apparent stratigraphic ranges.
Differences in taxonomic splitting between terrestrial vertebrates/insects and marine invertebrates can bias rate comparisons.
rationale: Comparing evolutionary turnover rates between land and sea organisms maps directly onto capture-mark-recapture and boundary-crosser rate estimators applied to the Paleobiology Database. Even after accounting for lower terrestrial completeness, existing datasets allow a direct statistical comparison of terrestrial versus marine turnover.

operationalization: Evaluate putative re-appearances of extinct species in the fossil record and living biota using high-dimensional morphometrics and genomic phylogenies to determine whether apparent reappearances are Lazarus taxa (continuous survival without fossilization) or homeomorphic convergence rather than identical re-evolution.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Stratigraphic gap distributions to identify Lazarus taxa versus genuine extinctions

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Genomic sequences of iterative ecomorphs to test genetic identity versus convergent evolution

obstacles: In the fossil record, taxonomy often defines temporally separated homeomorphs as distinct species a priori, creating circularity.
Distinguishing an unrecorded surviving lineage (Lazarus taxon) from extinction followed by iterative evolution requires dense stratigraphic and phylogenetic sampling.
rationale: While universal non-reappearance of a species (closely related to Dollo's law) is a foundational generalization, testing it strictly in fossils is complicated by Lazarus gaps and taxonomic conventions that split iterative morphotypes. Combining paleontological series with genomic data on iterative evolution provides strong partial resolution.

operationalization: Test whether genera and families defined in paleontological databases are monophyletic and stratigraphically continuous once sampling probabilities are accounted for, or whether apparent polyphyletic re-appearances reflect convergent grades that fail phylogenetic monophyly tests.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Stratigraphic ranges and gap statistics for fossil genera and families

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Cladistic matrices to test whether disjunct stratigraphic occurrences belong to a single clade or convergent lineages

obstacles: Modern cladistic taxonomy explicitly enforces monophyly, making the continuity of natural groups partly definitional unless evaluated on legacy pre-cladistic taxa.
rationale: The continuity of genera and families through time and the absence of true reappearance after clade extinction can be evaluated using stratigraphic gap analysis and phylogenetic tests on morphological and molecular datasets. Care must be taken to separate empirical continuity from modern monophyletic naming rules.

operationalization: Construct sampling-standardized species-per-genus and genus-per-family diversity trajectories across the lifespan of extinct clades to test whether their mean trajectory is unimodal (waxing to a single peak and then waning) rather than flat, multi-peaked, or step-like.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Time-binned species and genus counts within families across the Phanerozoic

obstacles: Secular variation in fossil sampling intensity and rock volume can distort clade spindle shapes if not standardized.
rationale: This claim directly describes the classic 'spindle diagram' or waxing-and-waning trajectory of clade diversity, which has been extensively quantified in analytical paleobiology (e.g., Foote 2007). Public occurrence data in the Paleobiology Database allow immediate, rigorous testing across thousands of genera and families.

operationalization: Quantify the distribution of extinction intensities across geological time bins to test whether all extinctions are gradual background processes or punctuated by global mass extinction events, and track regional last-appearance datums across continents in the Cenozoic.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Global and regional last appearances of species and genera across Phanerozoic stages

candidate_datasets.name: Neotoma Paleoecology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Spatially resolved radiocarbon-dated last appearances of Quaternary species across regions

obstacles: The Signor-Lipps effect makes sudden synchronous extinctions appear artificially gradual in local stratigraphic sections.
rationale: Both aspects of Darwin's claim—diachronous local extirpation prior to global extinction and the absence of global catastrophic sweeps—are directly testable with existing paleontological datasets. Spatial last-appearance data confirm diachronous range contraction for background and Quaternary extinctions, while stage-level turnover data clearly reveal major global mass extinctions that refute the strict anti-catastrophist part of the claim.

operationalization: Compute the center of gravity (skewness) of sampling-standardized diversity trajectories for extinct genera, families, and orders in the fossil record; a center of gravity below 0.5 (bottom-heavy clade shape) confirms faster origination and slower decline.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Stratigraphic occurrences of species and genera within higher taxa to measure clade trajectory asymmetry

obstacles: Paraphyletic taxonomic definitions in older literature artificially inflate bottom-heaviness compared with strictly monophyletic clades.
rationale: Clade diversity asymmetry (bottom-heavy versus top-heavy spindle diagrams, pioneered by Gould et al. 1977, 1987) is a standard quantitative metric in paleobiology. Public fossil occurrence databases provide comprehensive data to measure the relative duration of clade waxing versus waning.

operationalization: Measure trends in site occupancy, geographic range size, and specimen abundance in the time bins immediately preceding a species' last appearance in Cenozoic fossil databases and historical conservation records.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Occupancy and occurrence counts per time bin prior to last appearance in Cenozoic fossils

candidate_datasets.name: Neotoma Paleoecology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Pollen and vertebrate abundance trajectories preceding late Quaternary extinctions

candidate_datasets.name: IUCN Red List of Threatened Species
candidate_datasets.role: Population size and range contraction records for historically extirpated and extinct species

obstacles: Declining abundance immediately before last fossil appearance is partially confounded by the Signor-Lipps truncation effect unless sampling-standardized occupancy models are used.
rationale: Indeed, this exact claim serves as a textbook example of paleobiological and conservation hypothesis testing. Existing Cenozoic fossil databases and historical extinction records allow direct measurement of occupancy and abundance decline prior to extinction.

operationalization: Compare per-interval origination and extinction rates and test for diversity-dependent equilibrium (bounded versus unbounded Cenozoic standing diversity) using shareholder quorum subsampling on global fossil occurrences.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Global Phanerozoic and Cenozoic fossil occurrences for subsampled standing diversity and turnover rate estimation

obstacles: The Pull of the Recent and greater preservation of young unlithified sediments can create an apparent Cenozoic diversity surge if not fully corrected by subsampling.
rationale: Whether Cenozoic biodiversity is near equilibrium (with origination roughly balanced by extinction) or expanding exponentially is one of the most heavily analyzed questions in macroevolution. Publicly available fossil occurrence datasets and standard subsampling algorithms can test this directly.

operationalization: Test whether elevated speciation rates or the appearance of new congeneric species within a region significantly increases the extinction hazard of co-occurring species in the same genus compared to more distantly related ecologically similar species.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Co-occurrence and stratigraphic range overlap of congeneric species through time

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Phylogenetic trees of fossil clades to identify ancestor-descendant and sister-taxon pairs

obstacles: Directly identifying true parent-descendant species pairs in the fossil record is rare and controversial.
Shared environmental sensitivity often causes congeners to originate or go extinct together, confounding competitive displacement.
rationale: While diversity-dependent extinction within genera and clades can be tested statistically using fossil occurrence and phylogenetic datasets (e.g., Silvestro et al. clade competition models), demonstrating that new descendants directly exterminate their parent species rather than replacing them opportunistically after environmental change is limited by confounding variables.

operationalization: Compare the radiometric and magnetostratigraphic ages of marine biostratigraphic zone boundaries across distant ocean basins and latitudinal belts to quantify the degree of global synchroneity in marine faunal turnover.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Global marine fossil occurrences across paleolatitudes and sedimentary basins

candidate_datasets.name: Macrostrat
candidate_datasets.role: Chronostratigraphic correlation of marine formations tied to independent radiometric and geomagnetic age models

obstacles: If formations are dated solely by fossils, testing simultaneous faunal change would be circular; independent radiometric, magnetostratigraphic, or chemostratigraphic age controls are required.
rationale: Because modern geochronology links biostratigraphic zones to independent radiometric ages, geomagnetic reversals, and stable-isotope excursions, circularity is avoided. Publicly available stratigraphic and paleontological databases confirm that major marine faunal turnovers correlate globally within the resolution of geological stages.

operationalization: Correlate the geological age of fossil taxa with their morphological distance (patristic or character-space distance) from extant species, and measure the proportion of extant genera and families present in progressively older geological periods.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Geological ages of fossil species and the Lyellian percentage of extant taxa through time

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Morphological character matrices containing both fossil and extant taxa to compute character distance vs. geologic age

obstacles: So-called 'living fossils' (bradytelic lineages) exhibit low morphological divergence despite ancient origins, representing exceptions to the general rule.
rationale: Both taxonomic similarity (such as Lyellian percentages of extant genera/families) and morphological character distance between fossil and living organisms can be plotted directly against geological age using existing databases. The positive relationship between geological age and divergence from modern forms is cleanly and decisively testable.

operationalization: Measure pairwise morphological distances and nearest-neighbor gaps between extant orders and families in character space with and without extinct taxa included, testing whether adding fossils significantly reduces inter-clade morphological gaps.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Combined morphological character matrices of extant and extinct vertebrates, arthropods, and plants

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Taxonomic classification of extinct groups within the hierarchy of living and fossil life

obstacles: Soft-tissue characters that distinguish many extant higher taxa are rarely preserved in fossils, restricting comparisons to skeletal or hard-part characters.
rationale: Morphospace occupation analyses comparing extant-only versus total-group (extant plus fossil) datasets are standard in paleobiology. Public morphological matrices on MorphoBank directly allow testing whether stem-group fossils bridge the morphological intervals between living crown clades.

operationalization: For pairs of sister higher taxa (e.g., birds and crocodilians, mammals and reptiles), compute pairwise morphological character differences between their Paleozoic/Mesozoic members and compare them to the character differences between their extant members.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Discrete character matrices spanning early stem and modern crown members of major clades

obstacles: Fossil incompleteness means older taxa have more missing character states, requiring distance metrics normalized for observable characters.
rationale: Comparing pairwise character dissimilarity between early representatives of diverging clades and their extant representatives is straightforward using public cladistic matrices. Even when restricted to skeletal characters preserved in both fossils and living taxa, the convergence of character states toward the common ancestor in older strata is directly measurable.

operationalization: Calculate taxonomic similarity (e.g., Jaccard, Sorensen, or phylogenetic beta-diversity indices) between fossil assemblages as a function of the temporal separation (number of intervening stages or millions of years) between formations.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Stage-by-stage taxonomic occurrences across geological formations worldwide

candidate_datasets.name: Macrostrat
candidate_datasets.role: Stratigraphic superposition and age models of consecutive versus remote geological formations

obstacles: Biofacies shifts between consecutive formations (e.g., shallow marine to deep marine) can reduce similarity unless comparisons control for depositional environment.
rationale: Temporal distance-decay of taxonomic and phylogenetic similarity across geological stages is a foundational, easily computed metric in paleobiology. Public fossil and stratigraphic databases provide massive coverage to test and confirm that consecutive formations share far closer taxonomic affinities than temporally remote ones.

operationalization: Use proxy comparisons such as biotic interchange asymmetries between long-isolated archaic faunas and modern continental faunas, or compare functional performance traits (e.g., encephalization, metabolic proxies, biomechanical efficiency) across geological eras.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Fossil occurrences across historical biotic interchanges (e.g., Great American Biotic Interchange) as proxies for asymmetrical competition

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Distributions of phylogenetically basal ('relict') extant lineages relative to derived crown clades

obstacles: Direct competition experiments between extinct Eocene organisms and living organisms are physically impossible.
Using extant basal lineages or historical interchanges as proxies for extinct Eocene faunas introduces severe confounding variables.
rationale: As literally stated—placing an extinct Eocene fauna into direct competition with a modern fauna—this counterfactual prediction cannot be experimentally executed. It can only be evaluated indirectly through paleontological proxies like asymmetrical biotic interchanges or escalation in functional traits.

operationalization: Compute taxonomic and phylogenetic similarity between late Cenozoic (Neogene-Quaternary) fossil assemblages of each continent and the extant native biota of the same continent versus other continents.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Neogene and Quaternary fossil occurrences by continent and biogeographic realm

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Geographic distributions of extant terrestrial mammals, birds, and molluscs across continents

candidate_datasets.name: ASM Mammal Diversity Database
candidate_datasets.role: Continental distributions and taxonomy of living and recently extinct mammal clades

obstacles: Late Pleistocene megafaunal extinctions and recent intercontinental exchanges (such as the Great American Biotic Interchange) partially obscure in-situ succession for some clades.
rationale: The 'Law of Succession' within biogeographic realms is straightforward to operationalize by comparing cross-continental matrices of late Tertiary fossils and extant native species. Public paleontological and biodiversity databases cover the full taxonomic and geographic scope required for a decisive test.

operationalization: Perform variance partitioning (e.g., Multiple Regression on distance Matrices or Generalized Dissimilarity Modelling) on global species composition to test how much taxonomic beta-diversity among climatically matched regions (such as 25°-35° S in Australia, South Africa, and South America) is explained by climate versus geographic/biogeographic realm separation.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Global species occurrence records to compute taxonomic similarity across regions

candidate_datasets.name: Global Inventory of Floras and Traits
candidate_datasets.role: Regional plant checklists and bioclimatic variables across the globe

candidate_datasets.name: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information
candidate_datasets.role: Global climatological temperature, precipitation, and environmental layers

obstacles: Human-mediated introductions have homogenized some regional floras and faunas unless restricted to native species checklists.
rationale: Buffon's Law—that environmentally similar but geographically separated regions harbour taxonomically distinct biotas—maps directly onto modern macroecological variance partitioning and beta-diversity analyses. Comprehensive global checklists and climate layers are openly available and make the analysis fast and unambiguous.

operationalization: Correlate taxonomic and phylogenetic turnover (beta-diversity) between pairs of adjacent regions or marine basins with the permeability and geological age of intervening dispersal barriers (e.g., Isthmus of Panama, mountain chains, ocean basins, major rivers), controlling for geographic distance and climate.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Global terrestrial and marine species distributions across physical barriers

candidate_datasets.name: Global Inventory of Floras and Traits
candidate_datasets.role: Regional floristic inventories across continents, islands, and mountain dividers

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: Marine and freshwater fish distributions across oceanic, continental, and isthmus barriers

obstacles: Physical barriers often coincide with steep climatic gradients (e.g., rain shadows across mountain ranges), requiring statistical control for environmental distance.
rationale: Testing the effect of dispersal barriers and barrier age on biotic turnover is a standard macroecological and biogeographic analysis. Open global occurrence databases for terrestrial and marine taxa, paired with known geological barrier ages, allow a clean and decisive test.

operationalization: Compare phylogenetic and taxonomic relatedness (e.g., mean nearest taxon distance or congeneric/confamilial sharing) between species occupying different biomes on the same continent versus species occupying the same biome on different continents.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Species occurrences across habitats and continents to quantify within-continent vs. within-biome taxonomic affinity

candidate_datasets.name: Global Inventory of Floras and Traits
candidate_datasets.role: Regional plant checklists across biomes and continents

obstacles: Some ancient, globally distributed lineages show stronger biome conservatism (phylogenetic niche conservatism) across continents than recent adaptive radiations within a continent.
rationale: Whether species assemblages cluster more strongly by continent/biogeographic realm or by habitat/biome is a standard phylogenetic beta-diversity question. Public global species distribution and taxonomic databases allow immediate quantification across both terrestrial and marine realms.

operationalization: Test for spatial phylogenetic clustering (monophyly and patristic proximity of regional living and fossil taxa) and compare models of trait evolution driven by biotic diversification versus direct abiotic correlation across biogeographic realms.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Molecular sequence data to infer shared ancestry of regional clades independently of morphological convergence

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Regional fossil occurrences linking extinct and extant members of continental clades

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Geographic distributions of extant taxa across realms

obstacles: Phylogenetic trees built under evolutionary models assume common descent, so testing common ancestry requires evaluating tree-like signal (hierarchical character congruence) across independent genomic and morphological loci.
Separating natural selection driven by biotic interactions from selection driven by physical conditions is difficult in macroevolutionary datasets.
rationale: Independent genomic and paleontological datasets allow testing whether regional biotas share hierarchical genealogical signal (inheritance) rather than merely shared environmental adaptations. While partitioning the exact share of natural selection versus direct physical influence is more interpretive, the core phylogeographic and paleobiological predictions are strongly resolvable.

operationalization: Compare rates of morphological and genetic divergence and speciation in lineages that colonized isolated islands or continental fragments alongside their intact co-occurring community (e.g., land-bridge islands or whole-assemblage Pleistocene refugia) versus single colonists entering novel biotic communities.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Inventory of Floras and Traits
candidate_datasets.role: Endemism proportions and assemblage composition on land-bridge vs. oceanic islands

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Dated molecular phylogenies to compare divergence rates in whole-community vicariance vs. Disharmonic colonization

obstacles: Neutral genetic divergence (genetic drift) accumulates with isolation time regardless of biotic relations, contradicting a purely genetic reading though Darwin meant visible adaptive modification.
Land-bridge islands where communities arrive 'in a body' are also younger and closer to mainlands, confounding community intactness with isolation duration and gene flow.
rationale: Comparing morphological divergence and endemism between disharmonic island colonists (exposed to new biotic relations) and intact isolated communities (such as Pleistocene land-bridge islands or paleorefugia) is feasible with global island and phylogenetic datasets. However, island age, area, and ongoing gene flow covary with community intactness, limiting discriminating power.

operationalization: Calculate the proportion of families, subfamilies, and genera restricted to a single biogeographic realm, and test whether mean intrageneric phylogenetic or morphological similarity ('naturalness') is negatively correlated with the geographic range size or number of realms occupied by a genus.

candidate_datasets.name: Plants of the World Online
candidate_datasets.role: Global geographic distributions of all vascular plant genera and families

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Global occurrence records across taxonomic ranks for plants and animals

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Molecular sequence data to measure crown age and intrageneric genetic divergence

obstacles: What Darwin called 'the most natural genera' (those with the most closely allied species) maps onto young, tight monophyletic clades in modern taxonomy, whereas older taxonomy included polyphyletic 'dustbin' genera with wide ranges.
rationale: Measuring the proportion of higher taxa restricted to single biogeographic regions and correlating clade compactness (crown age or intrageneric divergence) with geographic extent is straightforward using global taxonomic and molecular databases.

operationalization: Test whether conspecific populations across a species' geographic range form a monophyletic lineage tracing to a single geographic origin in phylogeographic reconstructions, rather than arising polyphyletically from distinct local ancestors in separate regions.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Population-level and phylogeographic DNA sequence datasets across species ranges

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Geographic range continuity and occurrence records of extant species

obstacles: Recurrent polyploid speciation in plants and rare parallel ecological speciation can produce polyphyletic origins of the same nominal species or ecomorph in multiple localities.
rationale: Modern phylogeography and coalescent genetics directly test whether a species' populations trace back to a single geographic source (monophyletic single origin) or multiple independent origins. Massive public sequence repositories make this testable across thousands of plant and animal species, even identifying the rare exceptions such as recurrent allopolyploids.

operationalization: Evaluate global bathymetric, sea-level, and marine geological datasets over the late Cenozoic (Plio-Pleistocene, the lifespan of extant species) to determine whether deep ocean basins between separate continents and volcanic oceanic islands ever formed continuous subaerial land bridges.

candidate_datasets.name: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information
candidate_datasets.role: Global ocean bathymetry (ETOPO), marine sediment cores, and Quaternary sea-level reconstructions

obstacles: Continental shelf islands (e.g., Britain, Borneo) were joined to nearby continents during Pleistocene lowstands, which Darwin explicitly distinguished from true oceanic islands and intercontinental abyssal bridges.
rationale: Global bathymetry, ocean-floor geophysics, and Quaternary eustatic sea-level curves (~120-130 m maximum drop) conclusively resolve this claim. True oceanic islands and major separate continents are separated by abyssal depths of thousands of meters and were never connected by recent land bridges.

operationalization: Compile experimental seed buoyancy duration and saltwater germination survival data across regional floras, combined with surface ocean current drift velocities (~1-3 knots), to calculate the proportion of species whose dried seeds can remain afloat and viable for the time required to drift 900 miles (~20-40 days).

candidate_datasets.name: TRY Plant Trait Database
candidate_datasets.role: Seed buoyancy, dispersal syndrome (thalassochory/hydrochory), and seed coat traits across plant species

candidate_datasets.name: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information
candidate_datasets.role: Global surface ocean drifter and current velocity datasets

obstacles: Standardized saltwater immersion and flotation durations for dried seeds across entire non-coastal floras are only compiled for subsets of species in trait databases and scattered experimental papers.
rationale: The claim is quantitatively precise and easily operationalized, and ocean current velocities are well known. However, because large plant trait databases record dispersal syndrome and buoyancy for only a fraction of all species and rarely include standardized multi-week saltwater germination assays after drying, existing public data only partially cover the scope.

operationalization: Quantify floristic similarity (shared native species) and phylogenetic dispersal-event frequencies as a function of over-water distance between islands and continents, testing for a steep distance-decay threshold where species sharing drops near zero between distant continents while remaining substantial across a few hundred miles.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Inventory of Floras and Traits
candidate_datasets.role: Native vascular plant checklists and geographic distances for oceanic islands and continental regions worldwide

candidate_datasets.name: Plants of the World Online
candidate_datasets.role: Global native distributions of plant species across islands and continents

obstacles: Rare trans-oceanic long-distance dispersal events between distant continents do occur on macroevolutionary timescales, though at rates too low to homogenize continental floras.
rationale: Global island and continental floristic databases allow direct modeling of native species sharing and colonization probability against over-water distance. While molecular phylogenies show that occasional trans-oceanic dispersal between continents has occurred, existing data clearly resolve the steep distance decay that keeps continental floras distinct while populating nearby islands.

operationalization: Test whether disjunct arctic-alpine plant and animal populations across European and North American mountains occur as late Pleistocene fossils in intervening lowlands and exhibit shallow coalescent divergence times (dating to the Last Glacial Maximum / Holocene transition) in population-genetic datasets.

candidate_datasets.name: Neotoma Paleoecology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Late Pleistocene and Holocene pollen, plant macrofossil, and beetle records from lowland Europe and North America

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Chloroplast and nuclear phylogeographic datasets for arctic-alpine species (e.g., Dryas octopetala, Saxifraga oppositifolia)

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Modern disjunct arctic and alpine occurrence records

obstacles: Some alpine disjuncts result from recent post-glacial long-distance dispersal rather than continuous lowland vicariance, requiring coalescent demographic models to distinguish the two.
rationale: Darwin's glacial relict hypothesis for arctic-alpine disjunctions is directly testable and has been extensively resolved using both Quaternary lowland macrofossils/pollen (in Neotoma) and comparative phylogeography (in GenBank). The combination of fossil lowland occurrences during glacial stages and post-glacial genetic isolation provides a clean, decisive test.

operationalization: Estimate divergence times and ancestral geographic ranges for disjunct temperate sister clades between North America and Eurasia using dated molecular phylogenies, and cross-check against high-latitude Neogene/Pliocene fossil floras and faunas around the North Atlantic and Beringia.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: High-latitude Paleogene and Neogene fossil occurrences of temperate plant and animal genera

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Molecular sequence data for Holarctic temperate plant and animal genera to estimate transatlantic/Beringian divergence dates

candidate_datasets.name: Plants of the World Online
candidate_datasets.role: Taxonomic overlap at species vs. genus level between temperate North America and Europe

obstacles: Much of the boreotropical and Arcto-Tertiary exchange occurred in the Eocene-Miocene rather than strictly the Pliocene, though Beringian exchange continued into the Pliocene.
rationale: Both the descriptive pattern (high genus-level sharing with low species-level identity between temperate North America and Europe) and the historical mechanism (Cenozoic high-latitude circumpolar continuity followed by southward range shift and divergence) can be directly evaluated with public paleobotanical, paleozoological, and molecular clock datasets.

operationalization: Compare radiometrically and ice-core synchronized paleotemperature proxies (ice cores, marine foraminiferal delta-18O, speleothems, and cosmogenic nuclide moraine ages) across both hemispheres and latitudes during the Last Glacial Maximum and Pleistocene glacial cycles to test whether cooling was globally synchronous.

candidate_datasets.name: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information
candidate_datasets.role: World Data Service for Paleoclimatology ice-core, marine sediment, pollen, and glacial chronology datasets across both hemispheres

obstacles: Millennial-scale bipolar seesaw oscillations caused slight antiphase warmings between hemispheres within glacial stages, though orbital-scale glacial cooling was globally synchronous.
rationale: Global paleoclimatic proxy compilations at NOAA Paleoclimatology provide high-resolution, radiometrically dated temperature and ice-volume records from poles to tropics across both hemispheres. These data directly and conclusively resolve whether glacial cooling was globally simultaneous.

operationalization: Compare the floristic lists of high-elevation tropical and temperate mountain zones (alpine/subalpine belts) with temperate and boreal lowland floras to compute the percentage of shared species versus congeneric/confamilial distinct species.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Georeferenced and elevation-annotated plant occurrence records across tropical mountains and temperate lowlands

candidate_datasets.name: Global Inventory of Floras and Traits
candidate_datasets.role: Regional and montane floristic checklists worldwide

candidate_datasets.name: Plants of the World Online
candidate_datasets.role: Global taxonomy and distributions of montane and temperate vascular plant genera

obstacles: Defining the exact elevational boundary of 'lofty mountains' across latitudes requires standardizing by bioclimatic thermal belts (e.g., alpine treeline).
rationale: This empirical generalization about the floristic affinity between high mountains (such as the tropical Andes, East African mountains, and Himalayas) and temperate lowlands is easily quantified with modern global floristic databases. Data show high genus-level sharing alongside high species-level endemism on tropical mountains, matching the exact comparison needed.

operationalization: Use ancestral area reconstructions on dated plant phylogenies to compare the number of north-to-south versus south-to-north Plio-Pleistocene dispersal events across the tropics, and test whether directional asymmetry is explained by source land area/species pool size versus intrinsic competitive dominance.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Molecular phylogenies of bipolar and amphitropical plant lineages to infer dispersal direction and timing

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Latitudinal and elevational distributions of bipolar and montane plant clades

obstacles: Asymmetrical migration from larger to smaller land areas is expected under neutral mass/area effects (propagule pressure and species pool size) without invoking superior competitive perfection.
Darwin's concept of 'higher stage of perfection or dominating power' has no single agreed operational metric independent of colonization success itself.
rationale: The directional asymmetry of Plio-Pleistocene plant dispersal (predominantly north-to-south in bipolar and tropical-alpine floras) can be resolved using dated molecular phylogeographies. However, discriminating Darwin's competitive-dominance mechanism from simple neutral source-pool size and land-area geometry is difficult without circularity.

operationalization: Count the number and relative abundance of native European species naturalized in temperate South America (La Plata/Pampas) and Australia versus native South American and Australian species naturalized in Europe using global alien flora and fauna databases.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Naturalized Alien Flora
candidate_datasets.role: Comprehensive global inventory of naturalized alien plant species and their native vs. recipient regions

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Occurrence records and establishment status of introduced plants and animals in Europe, South America, and Australia

obstacles: Historical asymmetry in European colonial trade, agriculture, and propagule pressure strongly confounds biological invasibility if used to infer intrinsic superiority, though the empirical pattern itself is unambiguous.
rationale: As an empirical generalization about the asymmetrical numbers of naturalized species exchanged between Europe and the Southern Hemisphere, this claim maps directly onto the Global Naturalized Alien Flora (GloNAF) database. The asymmetry is quantified across thousands of species and can be tested in days.

operationalization: Examine pre-glacial (Cretaceous to Eocene/Oligocene) fossil pollen and macrofossils from Antarctica for southern-hemisphere disjunct genera (e.g., Nothofagus, Araucariaceae, Proteaceae, Podocarpaceae), and use dated molecular phylogenies to test whether divergences among South American, Australian, and New Zealand species reflect trans-Antarctic ancestral ranges and over-water dispersal.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Cretaceous and Paleogene fossil plant occurrences from Antarctica and southern continents

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Dated molecular phylogenies of classic Austral/Antarctic plant genera to test divergence timing vs. Gondwanan breakup

candidate_datasets.name: Plants of the World Online
candidate_datasets.role: Distributions of disjunct southern-hemisphere plant genera across South America, Australia, and New Zealand

obstacles: Southern-hemisphere disjunctions reflect a combination of Gondwanan continental vicariance (which Darwin did not know) and post-breakup trans-oceanic dispersal via a vegetated Paleogene Antarctica.
rationale: Antarctic paleobotanical records confirm a diverse temperate-to-warm flora on Antarctica prior to Oligocene-Miocene glaciation, and dated molecular phylogenies distinguish ancient Gondwanan vicariance from Paleogene/Neogene trans-Antarctic and over-water dispersal. Existing paleontological and molecular datasets resolve both the vegetated-Antarctica inference and the dispersal dynamics.

operationalization: Quantify the geographic range sizes (extent of occurrence and number of occupied continents/biogeographic realms) of freshwater plants, aquatic insects, freshwater molluscs, and crustaceans, and compare them against terrestrial counterparts in global biodiversity databases.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Global occurrence records of freshwater plants, molluscs, insects, and microcrustaceans

candidate_datasets.name: IUCN Red List of Threatened Species
candidate_datasets.role: Range polygons for global freshwater odonates, molluscs, decapods, and macrophytes

candidate_datasets.name: Plants of the World Online
candidate_datasets.role: Global native distributions of aquatic vascular plant species and genera

obstacles: Molecular barcoding has revealed that some supposedly cosmopolitan freshwater invertebrate species are complexes of cryptic sister species, shifting them from identical species to 'allied species' (which still fits the second clause of Darwin's claim).
rationale: Global range maps and occurrence records for freshwater macrophytes and invertebrates are readily available in GBIF, POWO, and IUCN. They allow a direct quantitative test of whether many freshwater species have trans-continental ranges and cosmopolitan genera.

operationalization: Query global freshwater fish checklists by river basin and continent to test (1) whether any strictly primary freshwater fish species is native to two distant continents, and (2) the distribution of species sharing across adjacent drainage basins within the same continent.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: Global taxonomy, salinity tolerance, native vs. introduced status, and drainage/continental distributions of all fish species

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: River-basin occurrence records of freshwater fishes worldwide

obstacles: Diadromous or euryhaline fishes (e.g., salmonids, anguillid eels, galaxiids) and high-latitude circumpolar species (e.g., Esox lucius across Eurasia and North America) must be distinguished from strictly freshwater fishes of distant continents.
rationale: Global drainage-basin checklists of freshwater fishes (such as FishBase and the global freshwater fish occurrence syntheses) cover virtually all known species with native/introduced flags. Testing intercontinental absence and intra-continental drainage sharing is trivial and decisive.

operationalization: Test whether geographic range size and genetic connectivity among isolated wetlands in freshwater plants and invertebrates correlate with traits enabling avian endozoochory/ectozoochory and alignment with migratory waterbird flyways, combined with field datasets of viable propagules recovered from waterbird feces and feathers.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Distributions of freshwater plants, invertebrates, and migratory waterbird flyways

candidate_datasets.name: TRY Plant Trait Database
candidate_datasets.role: Dispersal syndrome and seed traits of aquatic and wetland macrophytes

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Population genetic structure of aquatic plants and invertebrates along waterbird migration corridors

obstacles: Wind, hydrological connectivity during floods, and anthropogenic transport also disperse aquatic propagules, making it challenging to isolate the exact quantitative share ('mainly depends') attributable to waterbirds alone.
rationale: Numerous field sampling studies of viable seeds and invertebrate resting eggs in waterbird droppings/feathers, along with phylogeographic concordance with bird flyways, strongly support avian dispersal. However, because comparative field-recovery data are scattered across ecological supplements and confounded with wind and flood dispersal, the claim that wide ranges 'mainly depend' on birds is partially resolvable.

operationalization: Compare species-area relationships (intercept and slope of native species richness versus log area) between volcanic oceanic islands and equal-sized mainland or continental-shelf regions while controlling for climate (temperature, precipitation, and net primary productivity) in regression models.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Inventory of Floras and Traits
candidate_datasets.role: Native plant species richness, island geology (oceanic vs. continental), area, and climate for thousands of islands and mainland regions

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Vertebrate and invertebrate species richness across oceanic islands and mainland regions

obstacles: Human-caused prehistoric extinctions on oceanic islands (especially of birds and reptiles) have further depressed extant native richness below pre-human baselines.
rationale: Comparing species-area curves and climatic covariates between oceanic islands and mainland areas is a cornerstone of island biogeography. The GIFT database and global vertebrate datasets contain all required variables (geologic origin, area, climate, and native richness) for a clean, immediate test.

operationalization: Compare the proportion of native species that are single-region endemics on oceanic islands versus continental regions of comparable area and latitude.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Inventory of Floras and Traits
candidate_datasets.role: Total native and endemic vascular plant species counts for oceanic islands and continental regions globally

candidate_datasets.name: IUCN Red List of Threatened Species
candidate_datasets.role: Global distributions of terrestrial vertebrates to compute island vs. mainland endemism proportions

obstacles: Paleoendemics (relictual lineages that went extinct on continents) contribute alongside neoendemics (in-situ speciation) to total island endemism, though phylogenetic dating can separate the two.
rationale: Proportional endemism on oceanic islands relative to equal-sized mainland areas is directly tabulated in global floristic and vertebrate databases such as GIFT. The empirical pattern is overwhelmingly clear and can be tested with standard statistical models in days.

operationalization: Within oceanic archipelagos, compare the proportion of endemic species across taxonomic or ecological groups that differ in vagility and immigration frequency (e.g., pelagic seabirds and littoral marine molluscs vs. terrestrial land snails and flightless insects), and test whether high-dispersal groups have lower endemism.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Island occurrence records across taxonomic classes differing in dispersal ability

candidate_datasets.name: IUCN Red List of Threatened Species
candidate_datasets.role: Endemism and migratory/dispersal status of seabirds, waterbirds, and landbirds on oceanic islands

candidate_datasets.name: Global Inventory of Floras and Traits
candidate_datasets.role: Island plant endemism paired with dispersal syndrome traits

obstacles: Low endemism in vagile, frequently immigrating groups is explained in modern evolutionary biology primarily by ongoing gene flow preventing reproductive isolation rather than solely by Darwin's mechanism of 'undisturbed mutual relations'.
rationale: The empirical relationship between dispersal facility (immigration rate) and proportional endemism across taxa on the same island is readily testable with existing island checklists and trait databases. While modern theory attributes the lack of modification in frequent immigrants mainly to gene flow rather than undisturbed biotic relations, the comparative prediction across groups is strongly resolvable.

operationalization: Use dated molecular phylogenies and global plant growth-form databases to identify evolutionary transitions from herbaceous continental ancestors to woody shrub/tree habits on oceanic islands (insular woodiness), and test whether oceanic islands have a significantly higher proportion of derived woody species in predominantly herbaceous families (e.g., Asteraceae, Campanulaceae, Echium) than mainlands.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Inventory of Floras and Traits
candidate_datasets.role: Growth-form distributions (herb, shrub, tree) and taxonomic family composition on oceanic islands vs. continents

candidate_datasets.name: TRY Plant Trait Database
candidate_datasets.role: Plant height and woodiness traits across insular and continental species

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Molecular phylogenies confirming repeated independent transitions from continental herbs to insular shrubs and trees

obstacles: Multiple selective pressures on islands (such as year-round moderate climate lacking frost, drought resistance, or reduced herbivory) compete with Darwin's taller-stature competition hypothesis to explain why insular woodiness evolves.
rationale: Secondary 'insular woodiness'—the evolution of shrubs and trees from herbaceous colonists on oceanic islands—is a famous macroevolutionary phenomenon with dedicated global datasets (e.g., Zizka et al. 2022, integrated with GIFT and TRY) and hundreds of phylogenetic reconstructions. Both the overrepresentation of woody forms in herbaceous clades on islands and the direction of ancestral state transitions are directly resolvable.

operationalization: Cross-reference global amphibian distribution databases with geological classifications of islands (volcanic de novo oceanic islands never connected to continental crust versus continental-fragment/land-bridge islands) to test whether native amphibians are absent from true oceanic islands while introduced amphibians establish populations there.

candidate_datasets.name: AmphibiaWeb
candidate_datasets.role: Global taxonomy and native versus introduced geographic distributions of all amphibians (frogs, toads, salamanders, caecilians)

candidate_datasets.name: IUCN Red List of Threatened Species
candidate_datasets.role: Global range maps of amphibians coded by origin (native vs. introduced) across islands

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Occurrence records of native and naturalized amphibians on oceanic archipelagos (e.g., Hawaii, Galapagos, Mascarenes, Azores)

obstacles: Islands must be carefully classified geologically (excluding ancient Gondwanan continental fragments like New Zealand, Seychelles, or Fiji, or infrequent Holocene human translocations) to test true de novo oceanic islands.
rationale: Global amphibian databases (AmphibiaWeb and IUCN) provide complete species-level coverage of native and introduced amphibians across all islands, and physiological data on amphibian osmoregulation in seawater are well established. Both the natural absence on true oceanic islands and the thriving of introduced species (e.g., in Hawaii, Guam, and Puerto Rico/Caribbean islands) are immediately verifiable.

operationalization: Query global mammal distribution databases for all non-volant, non-marine native mammal species occurring on islands located >300 miles (~480 km) from the nearest continent or large continental island, and compare with records of introduced terrestrial mammals on those same islands.

candidate_datasets.name: ASM Mammal Diversity Database
candidate_datasets.role: Global taxonomy and native geographic distributions of all living and recently extinct mammal species

candidate_datasets.name: IUCN Red List of Threatened Species
candidate_datasets.role: Global range polygons of terrestrial mammals coded by native vs. introduced status

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Quaternary fossil occurrences of endemic insular rodents (e.g., Galapagos, Canary Islands) to check rare exceptions

obstacles: A tiny number of sigmodontine rodents (e.g., Megaoryzomys and Nesoryzomys on the Galapagos, ~600 miles from South America) did raft across >300 miles, providing a rare empirical exception that is itself documented in existing databases.
rationale: This quantitative biogeographic claim has an explicit distance threshold (300 miles) and clear taxonomic scope (native non-flying terrestrial mammals). Complete global mammal distribution datasets (ASM Mammal Diversity Database and IUCN) and island geographic coordinates allow an exact, definitive test of both the near-universal rule and its rare rodent-rafting exceptions.

operationalization: Calculate the proportion of oceanic islands inhabited by native bats (Chiroptera) versus native non-volant terrestrial mammals, and compute the proportion of oceanic island bat species that are single-island or archipelago endemics.

candidate_datasets.name: ASM Mammal Diversity Database
candidate_datasets.role: Global distributions and island endemism of all extant and recently extinct Chiroptera species

candidate_datasets.name: IUCN Red List of Threatened Species
candidate_datasets.role: Global range maps of bat species across oceanic islands

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: Occurrence records of bats on remote oceanic islands worldwide

obstacles: A few of the most extreme, small, or cold oceanic islands lack even native bats, making 'almost every island' slightly dependent on minimum island size and latitude thresholds.
rationale: Global mammal checklists and range maps in the ASM Mammal Diversity Database and IUCN Red List provide comprehensive coverage of native bats across oceanic islands (such as Hawaii, Galapagos, New Zealand, Mascarenes, Samoa, and Azores). The contrast between widespread bat presence/endemism and non-volant mammal absence on remote islands is completely resolvable with existing data.
